question: Let $$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.$$ Prove that if two matrices $B$ and $C$ are inverses of $A$, then they must be equal, and use the defining equation for an inverse to determine the unique inverse of $A$.
explanation:
Uniqueness of the Inverse

Suppose $B$ and $C$ are both inverses of $A$. Then, by the definition of inverse, $$AB=BA=I$$ and $$AC=CA=I$$ Using the associative property of matrix multiplication and the identity matrix, $$B=BI=B(AC)=(BA)C=IC=C$$ Hence, if an inverse of $A$ exists, it is unique.

Determination of the Inverse

Let the inverse be $$X=\begin{bmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{bmatrix}$$ Using $AX=I$, $$\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$$ Therefore, $$\begin{bmatrix}p+r&q+s\\p+2r&q+2s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$$ Comparing corresponding elements gives $p+r=1$, $p+2r=0$, $q+s=0$ and $q+2s=1$. Subtracting the first equation from the second gives $r=-1$, and therefore $p=2$. Similarly, subtracting $q+s=0$ from $q+2s=1$ gives $s=1$, and hence $q=-1$. Thus, $$X=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$$

Verification

Now, $$XA=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=I$$ Thus $AX=XA=I$, so the inverse exists. From the uniqueness established above, this inverse is the only inverse of $A$. Therefore, $$A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$$.

options.B: $A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$, and any two inverses $B$ and $C$ satisfy $B=C$
options.C: $A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$, and any two inverses $B$ and $C$ satisfy $B=C$
